answers.answer: A bucket contains objects. An object contains bytes and metadata; its key identifies it within its bucket. Metadata describes the object, for example content type, whereas application fields, relationships and ownership records belong to a separate application model. In a flat namespace slashes are name characters: console folders group keys sharing a prefix, not filesystem directories. Changing that prefix changes affected object names, commonly by copies and deletes, not one atomic directory rename. Upload report bytes and metadata to the object store under bucket and key; the database stores the application record and object reference. Later read that reference and request the object by key. Upload and database commit are separate operations, not one transaction. Publish the reference as ready only after confirming the intended object; a pending record may exist earlier if readers cannot mistake it for completion. An uncertain upload stays unresolved until verified. Successful upload with failed database commit can leave an unreferenced object; an early ready reference can point to missing bytes. The application must recover through retrying publication or cleaning up an object established to be unnecessary. Listing does not make these writes atomic.

evidence.quote: Each object contains bytes and metadata; its key identifies it within that bucket.
Console folders group keys by a shared beginning, called a prefix; they are not filesystem directories.
The object upload and database commit are separate operations.
Confirm the intended object before making a reference available as ready to readers.

answers.answer: Supply a complete replacement at the same key even when changing only a few bytes. S3 reads see complete old or new bytes, never a mixture; GCS serves the old object until replacement completes and then the new object. The completed replacement is current, though an overlapping read may have observed the previous object. Atomicity does not stop another writer replacing it. With versioning and other retention disabled, do not expect recovery of previous bytes. These are product-specific guarantees, not universal promises of every object store; verify the chosen operations and protections.

evidence.quote: changing a few bytes means supplying a complete replacement at the same key.
a concurrent read sees the complete old or new object, never a mixture.
With versioning and other retention protections disabled, do not expect to retrieve the old object after replacement.

answers.answer: An exact-key read retrieves one object; prefix listing enumerates names with a common beginning. Finding customer-owned approved records requires application records or a suitable index because listing does not filter arbitrary fields inside objects. Listing and inspecting objects adds requests, transferred data and latency as the collection grows. With no intervening change, current S3/GCS strong read-after-write and listing consistency reflect a successful upload in later reads and listings; this is provider-specific, and an HTTP cache may still serve an older copy. A consistent request can fail: freshness is not availability. Listing pages are not promised to form a frozen snapshot while objects change; neither strong listings nor single-key updates create transactions over multiple keys or the application database. Overlapping writes cannot be ordered by response arrival alone to determine the final value; observe stored state under provider rules.

evidence.quote: An exact-key request retrieves one object. A prefix listing enumerates names with a shared beginning.
With no intervening change, a successful upload is reflected in subsequent reads and listings.
Separate pages are not promised to form one frozen snapshot while objects change.
When writes to one key overlap, response arrival order alone does not identify the final object.

answers.answer: Yes, an upload may complete while its response is lost. An unconditional retry can replace a newer object another writer stored at that key. Before publishing ready, establish that the expected identity and content are stored using an acknowledged result or verification under documented semantics. Existence alone means some object exists, not the intended upload. A later read describes the state it observes; intervening writes mean it does not necessarily identify the earlier request that produced it or prove the original request outcome. A supported create-if-absent condition protects an existing live object from replacement, and an expected-version condition permits replacement only of the intended version; the check is part of the operation. A rejected condition does not prove your bytes are stored, and losing a conditional-upload response still leaves uncertainty. S3 and GCS offer different APIs and details, so follow the documented protection and recovery path rather than assuming universal APIs or safe retries.

evidence.quote: A timeout does not prove that nothing was stored.
Finding the key proves only that some object exists.
An expected-version condition allows replacement only of the version the caller intended.
A rejected condition does not prove your bytes are stored. A lost response to a conditional upload is still uncertain.

answers.answer: Durability concerns retaining intact data over time; availability concerns access when requested. Durable data can be temporarily unreachable, and neither target proves a particular upload response arrived. Redundant storage protects against hardware failure. S3/GCS store data redundantly before confirming successful writes, but completing that server-side write does not ensure its response reaches the caller. Multiple devices within one zone need not survive loss of the zone; check storage class and placement. Redundancy does not undo intentional overwrites or deletions. Versioning may retain earlier versions and other retention/recovery features may preserve removed bytes. Check protections enabled, whether configuration changes have taken effect, and whether the required data is still retained. Recovery is neither automatic nor permanent merely because durability is high.

evidence.quote: Concerns keeping stored data intact over time.
Concerns being able to access data when requested.
Multiple devices in one zone do not necessarily protect against losing that whole zone.
Check which protections are enabled, whether configuration changes have taken effect, and whether the needed data is still retained.

answers.answer: The store authorizes presented credentials against its policies; it does not automatically consult application ownership records. The application must check whether the requesting user may access this resource before retrieving bytes or granting download access. A broad API credential can therefore retrieve another user's object from a private bucket if that check is skipped. A hard-to-guess key is an identifier, not permission enforcement. Limit credentials to needed operations and resources; untrusted clients holding broad credentials could directly bypass application restrictions within that scope. Do not assume immediate policy revocation: GCS documents propagation delays, so check provider behavior. Use object storage for media/export bytes fetched by key as whole objects. Use a database for frequently updated field-queryable records, relationships and transactions. Use block storage for an attached disk-like volume where a database engine reads/writes small ranges. Use shared file storage for directories and file operations shared by multiple machines. Use a CDN to cache/deliver popular assets close to users, reducing origin traffic and latency; object storage can hold the authoritative durable origin, and CDN does not replace it or the database. Whole-object replacement and request overhead make object storage a poor default for frequent small in-place changes. A bucket lacks the database capabilities and application permission checks, even with object metadata. Large size is not required: small objects are allowed.

evidence.quote: The object store authorizes the credentials presented on a request against its policies.
A hard-to-guess key is still an identifier, not a permission check.
GCS documents that granting and revoking access can take time to propagate.
Whole-object replacement and request overhead make it a poor default for frequent small in-place edits.
The CDN does not replace the authoritative durable copy or the application database.
